summary: Updates RFC 1035 by limiting the QDCOUNT field in DNS messages with OPCODE 0 (QUERY) to a maximum of one. It also specifies how to behave when messages with disallowed values are received.

eli5.summary: A DNS question form has a spot to say how many questions. Everyone really uses one, so this rules that only one is allowed.

questions: can a dns query have multiple questions
what does formerr mean in dns
subtitle: A DNS query message carries at most one question, and anything else gets a FORMERR reply.

tldr.problem: RFC 1035 says the Question section holds QDCOUNT (usually 1) entries, but never says in firm terms what happens when a query carries more than one question. That leaves the other header fields, such as AA and RCODE, with no clear meaning.
tldr.mechanism: A DNS message with OPCODE = 0 MUST NOT have QDCOUNT greater than 1. If one arrives anyway, it is treated as incorrectly formatted and the response RCODE MUST be 1 (FORMERR).
tldr.outcome: This removes an ambiguity in the base DNS specification and updates RFC 1035. Firewalls should return FORMERR for QDCOUNT > 1 but must not treat QDCOUNT = 0 as malformed.

today: RFC 9619 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1035. The listed metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why QDCOUNT Needs a Rule
sections.content:
Every DNS message has a header with a field called QDCOUNT, an unsigned 16-bit value that says how many questions are in the Question section. In principle it could hold a large range of values.

For ordinary queries and responses (messages with OPCODE = 0), other parts of the protocol already limit the useful values to 0 or 1. Response fields such as AA and RCODE have no defined meaning when a message contains several questions, because there is no way to say which question they refer to.
sections.eli5: The form has a box for how many questions you ask. You could write any number, but the answer sheet only has room to reply to one question at a time.

sections.title: What RFC 1035 Already Said
sections.content:
Section 4.1.2 of RFC 1035 says the Question section "contains QDCOUNT (usually 1) entries". That wording is not a firm requirement, because the RFC was written long before the BCP 14 key words such as MUST were in use.

The text elsewhere refers to "the question" in the singular. The AA bit, for example, says the responding name server is an authority for the domain name "in question section". The only documented exception was the old IQuery operation, whose response could carry zero, one or multiple names, and that operation was obsoleted by RFC 3425.

The appendix concludes that nothing in RFC 1035 explains how AA or RCODE should be read when a message has more than one question. A sender of such a query can have no expectations, and a receiver of such a response has no guidance.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook said the form usually has one question and talked about it as if there was only one. But it never said plainly that more was not allowed.

sections.title: The New Rule
sections.content:
A DNS message with OPCODE = 0 MUST NOT include a QDCOUNT greater than 1. It follows that its Question section MUST NOT contain more than one question.

This does not forbid a QDCOUNT of 0. The document points to cases in older RFCs where that is legitimate: a DNS Cookies request (RFC 7873) that asks for a Server Cookie without any specific question, and later messages of a multi-message AXFR response (RFC 5936).
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: one question per form, no more. An empty form is still fine in a few special cases.

sections.title: What to Do With a Bad Message
sections.content:
A message with OPCODE = 0 and QDCOUNT > 1 MUST be treated as incorrectly formatted. The RCODE in the response MUST be set to 1, which is FORMERR.

Middleboxes such as firewalls that inspect DNS messages to drop unwanted traffic SHOULD treat OPCODE = 0 with QDCOUNT > 1 as malformed and return a FORMERR response as well. They MUST NOT treat OPCODE = 0 with QDCOUNT = 0 as malformed. The RFC points to Section 4 of RFC 8906 for further guidance.
sections.eli5: If someone hands in a form with too many questions, you stamp it "badly filled in" and send it back. A guard at the door should do the same, but must let blank forms through.

sections.title: How Other Opcodes Handle It
sections.content:
The appendix checks every other OPCODE. For NOTIFY (OPCODE 4), RFC 1996 says a request has QDCOUNT > 0 but otherwise treats the question tuple as a single item. For UPDATE (OPCODE 5), RFC 2136 renames the field ZOCOUNT and allows exactly one record in the Zone Section.

DNS Stateful Operations (OPCODE 6, RFC 8490) sets all four section counts to zero to stay compatible with the 12-octet DNS header. OPCODE 1 (IQUERY) is obsolete, OPCODE 2 (STATUS) is not specified, and OPCODE 3 is reserved. That leaves OPCODE 0 as the one case lacking clear language.
sections.eli5: The authors checked all the other kinds of forms. They already had clear counts, so only the plain question form needed fixing.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The security section is brief. The document clarifies the DNS specification and aims to improve interoperability between implementations, and removing ambiguity "seems well-aligned with security hygiene". It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: When everyone follows the same clear rule, there are fewer surprises, and fewer surprises are safer.
